A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices support reliable comparison, including matching material relocated in v3.

before.justification: v2 reports original online-learning and repeated-game experiments, regret-loss training results, and appendix ablations and numerical validations.

after.justification: v3 retains original empirical results and adds longer-horizon evaluations, a stochastic-bandit comparison, and raw-versus-summarized-history experiments.

M1.justification: The regret-loss objective, attention architectures, and bandit loss re-weighting remain unchanged. Sections 3.2–3.4 introduce a summarized-history input variant supplying cumulative per-action losses instead of the complete sequence, a limited adaptation of the LLM inference procedure.

E1.justification: Coverage remains within synthetic online learning and repeated games. v3 adds a hard Bernoulli stochastic-bandit instance in Appendix A and an alternating-then-constant adversarial loss sequence in Section 3.4. Existing full-information, bandit-feedback, non-stationary, and multiplayer settings are retained.

E2.justification: Table 2 introduces comparisons with Thompson Sampling, UCB, and the cited successful prompt configuration of Krishnamurthy et al. (2024), alongside unreweighted Naive variants. These constitute a substantive expansion beyond the earlier comparisons. The longer-horizon comparison also adds GPT-4o and removes Mixtral and Llama from that experiment; their shorter-horizon results remain.

E3.justification: v2's 50-round horizon study is replaced by 100-round Uniform/Gaussian and 200-round Linear/Sine experiments, with an additional 500-round summarized-input evaluation. New experiments compare raw and summarized histories and evaluate stochastic-bandit median reward, suffix failures, and uniform-like behavior. These substantially extend the evaluation design rather than establish same-setting performance improvements.

E4.justification: v3 adds controlled analyses of information lost through history summarization (Figure C.4) and the contribution of bandit loss re-weighting (Table 2). It also substantially extends horizon robustness testing, replacing the earlier 50-round study. Existing prompt ablations, quantal-response fitting, and regret-loss parameter ablations are retained.

E5.justification: Section 3.4 adds a one-sided independent t-test comparing raw and summarized histories, reporting p = 1.2 × 10^-157. The trend-checking framework explicitly restricts application to non-negative regret sequences and defines its decreasing-pattern criterion. Existing repetition counts and the environment-based error-bar convention remain; no increase in repeated runs is established.

E6.justification: v3 adds substantial results for longer horizons, the switching sequence, and the hard bandit instance, while removing v2's 50-round results. For example, Table 2 newly reports GPT-4o median rewards of 0.475 with re-weighting versus 0.455 for Naive, and suffix-failure frequencies of 0 versus 0.2. The retained 25-round plots and dynamic-regret table values are unchanged.

T1.justification: v3 corrects the binomial summand in Proposition 1's proof and derivative factors and indices in the linear-attention proof, including Equation (21) becoming Equation (E.11). It also omits v2's explicit support-interior assumption from Section 5.3. The principal regret bounds and attention-to-FTRL results are retained and largely relocated rather than newly established.

C1.justification: The introduction narrows broad no-regret language to sublinear regret on a large portion of tested instances, emphasizes full-information feedback, and explicitly disclaims certifying current LLMs as universal no-regret learners. The abstract also specifies single-layer self-attention for the optimization guarantee. The central contributions remain the same.

C2.justification: New interpretation explains why summaries can discard ordering information needed for adversarial sequences while serving as useful statistics in i.i.d. settings. Appendix A distinguishes exploration failures from adversarial regret and explains the role of externally supplied re-weighted feedback. Figure 4.1 adds a tentative explanation that quantal-response-like behavior may not always be triggered.

D1.justification: v3 documents cumulative-loss summarization, temperature 0 for the switching-sequence comparison, and the hard bandit's Bernoulli rewards, five actions, 100 rounds, and 0.2 reward gap. The existing optimizer, architecture, epoch, and batch-size details are retained in Appendix E.11, corresponding to v2 Appendix D.8.

R1.justification: New Appendix A substantially positions the work against concurrent Krishnamurthy et al. (2024), comparing feedback, exploration, prompts, horizons, and failure criteria. Appendix D.7 expands the comparison with Liu et al. (2023c). Additional citation changes include Feder et al. (1992) for the new counterexample and removal of the temporal-difference study by Wang et al. (2024).

P1.justification: Sections 3–5 undergo substantial condensation and reorganization. Background observations, non-stationary and bandit discussions, formal theorem statements, and supporting explanations move into reorganized appendices. The abstract, introduction, section headings, and explanatory passages are revised to emphasize the narrower empirical claims and distinguish the theoretical contributions.

P2.justification: The display structure changes substantially: v2 Table 1 becomes appendix Table 3, and Figures 2, 5, and 6 move to Figures C.1–C.3. v3 adds two tables and Figure C.4, replaces the horizon-study figure, relocates the interaction diagram, and revises captions and prompt-box layout. Most retained plot content is unchanged.

improvement.justification: Longer-horizon evaluations and the controlled comparisons in Figure C.4 and Table 2 strengthen evidence about robustness and applicability. More qualified claims better reflect the finite-instance findings. However, replacing the 50-round study removes longer-horizon evidence for open-source models, and the core method and guarantees remain largely unchanged. The added evidence and clearer framing support a limited net improvement.
